title: Word Search
directAnswer: Determine whether `word` can be spelled by a path of adjacent cells in the grid (no cell reused). The canonical answer is DFS + backtracking from every cell: match a letter, mark the cell visited, recurse into the 4 neighbours, then UN-mark on the way out. The in-place '#' marking trick avoids a separate visited matrix; restoring the cell after the recursion is the backtracking discipline that lets other paths reuse it.

remember.pattern: Grid DFS + backtracking (choose → explore → un-choose) with visited-marking
remember.formula:
def dfs(r, c, k):
    if k == len(word): return True
    if out_of_bounds or board[r][c] != word[k]: return False
    tmp, board[r][c] = board[r][c], '#'      # choose / mark visited
    found = any(dfs(r+dr, c+dc, k+1) for 4 dirs)  # explore
    board[r][c] = tmp                          # un-choose / restore
    return found
rules: Mark the current cell visited **before** recursing and **restore** it after — the restore is what lets sibling paths legally reuse the cell.
Use the in-place '#' (sentinel) trick to avoid a separate visited matrix; just remember to put the original letter back.
Check bounds and the letter match at the **top** of the DFS so the recursion is self-guarding — callers don't pre-validate neighbours.
Return `True` immediately on the first successful neighbour (short-circuit); don't keep exploring once the word is found.
Launch a DFS from **every** cell — the word can start anywhere; prune by only starting where `board[r][c] == word[0]`.
whenToUse: Search a grid/matrix for a path matching a sequence under adjacency rules
Each cell may be used at most once per path (need visited-marking)
Exploring connected neighbours (4- or 8-directional) with the option to abandon dead branches
'Does a path exist?' or 'find/count paths' on a 2-D board
antiSignals: Cells can be revisited freely → plain BFS/DFS reachability, no backtracking restore needed
Searching for MANY words at once → build a Trie (that's Word Search II)
Shortest path / fewest steps → BFS, not exhaustive DFS
No adjacency constraint, just membership → hash set, not a grid walk
remember.takeaway: Word Search is the canonical grid-backtracking problem: DFS with mark-on-enter / restore-on-exit. The same choose/explore/un-choose discipline drives Number of Islands variants, Word Search II (add a Trie), and rat-in-a-maze path problems. The restore step is the one line beginners forget and the one interviewers watch for.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can write a clean recursive grid DFS with correct backtracking — marking a cell visited on entry and restoring it on exit — and whether you launch the search from every valid starting cell.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Forgetting to restore the cell after the recursion (so a letter consumed on one branch stays blocked for others), or using a path that revisits the same cell because there's no visited-marking at all.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Use the in-place '#' marking trick to avoid an O(mn) visited matrix, prune starts where the first letter doesn't match, and mention the frequency / reverse-word optimisations and the Trie generalisation (Word Search II).

problemStatement:
Given an `m x n` grid of characters `board` and a string `word`, return `true` if `word` exists in the grid.

The word can be constructed from letters of **sequentially adjacent cells**, where adjacent cells are horizontally or vertically neighboring. **The same letter cell may not be used more than once.**
constraints: board and word consist of only lowercase and uppercase English letters
understanding: We're asked a yes/no question: can we trace `word` letter by letter through the grid, stepping only to up/down/left/right neighbours and never stepping on a cell we've already used in this path? We must try starting from every cell, and the no-reuse rule is what forces backtracking (mark a cell, recurse, then free it).

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can a single cell be reused within the same path?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. Each letter cell is used at most once per path — that's exactly why we mark cells visited and restore them on backtrack.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What counts as 'adjacent' — diagonals too?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Only the 4 orthogonal neighbours (up, down, left, right). No diagonal moves.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the word start anywhere in the grid?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — there's no fixed start. We launch a DFS from every cell whose letter equals word[0].

clarifyingQuestions.question: How big is the input?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Tiny: at most a 6×6 grid and a 15-character word. Exponential DFS with pruning is comfortably fast, so we optimise for clarity and correct backtracking.

examples.explanation: A(0,0)→B(0,1)→C(0,2)→C(1,2)→E(2,2)→D(2,1) traces the word through adjacent cells with no reuse.
S(1,3)→E(2,3)→E(2,2) works. The two E cells are distinct, so the no-reuse rule is satisfied.
After A→B→C, the second B would require reusing the first B's cell, which is forbidden — no path exists.

diagrams.title: The grid-DFS decision tree
diagrams.caption: Each node is a (cell, letter-index) state. We choose a cell, mark it '#', explore 4 neighbours, then restore it. The path that completes the word is highlighted; branches that hit a mismatch or a visited cell are pruned.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Enumerate All Paths Without Pruning
approaches.whenToMention: Mention it to frame the search space and the no-reuse requirement, then reject it — it doesn't prune on letter mismatch and re-allocates visited state wastefully.

complexity.space: O(m·n) visited matrix per call + O(L) recursion

hints: The literal idea: from each starting cell, walk out in all 4 directions building a string, and compare the full L-length string to `word` at the end.
To honour no-reuse you carry a visited set; without pruning you keep walking even after the prefix already disagrees with `word`.
This explores enormous numbers of length-L paths that diverged from `word` at the very first letter — checking the match only at the end is the waste.
approaches.complexityReasoning: From each of m·n cells you branch up to 4 ways for L levels (4^L paths), and checking the match only at the end means mismatched prefixes are explored fully; a freshly allocated visited matrix per start adds more overhead.
approaches.explanation:
The most literal approach: from every cell, generate every length-`L` walk over adjacent, non-reused cells, materialise the string it spells, and compare to `word` at the end.

**Why it's a reasonable first framing.** It correctly captures the search space — paths through the grid — and the no-reuse constraint via a visited set. Saying it out loud shows you understand the shape of the problem before optimising.

**Why it's wasteful.** It checks the letter match only after building a full path, so it explores every one of the ~4^L walks even when the prefix disagrees with `word` at letter 0. A path starting on a cell that doesn't even equal `word[0]` is pursued to full depth. Carrying a separate visited matrix that you allocate per start (instead of marking in place) adds constant-factor overhead and memory churn.

**The fix it points to.** Fuse the match-check into the walk: validate `board[r][c] == word[k]` at the *top* of each recursive step and bail the instant it fails. That single change converts the blind 4^L enumeration into a sharply pruned DFS, and reusing the board itself as the visited marker removes the extra matrix.
approaches.insight: Generate-all-paths-then-compare separates 'walk' from 'check'. The optimal DFS fuses them — it refuses to extend a path the moment a letter disagrees — which prunes the overwhelming majority of branches before they grow.

java.explanation: Match is checked only when the path is full length L, so mismatched prefixes are walked completely first.

python.line: done = path == word                      # compare only at full length
python.explanation: We compare only at length L — every doomed prefix is explored to the end before being rejected.

python.line: if walk(r, c, "", set()):                 # fresh visited per start
python.explanation: Launching from every cell with a fresh set, with no first-letter prune, wastes walks on cells that can't start the word.

diagrams.title: Blind enumeration starts everywhere
diagrams.caption: Without a first-letter prune, full walks are launched even from cells that can't begin the word (red), and matches are only checked at the leaves.

edgeCases.behavior: Single cell matches at full length 1 → returns true. Works, but the lack of a first-letter prune is irrelevant only because the grid is 1×1.

pitfalls: Comparing the path string only at full length means mismatched prefixes are explored completely.
Allocating a fresh visited matrix per starting cell churns memory unnecessarily.
No first-letter prune launches full walks from cells that can't start the word.

approaches.name: DFS + Backtracking with In-Place Marking (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Phrase it as 'DFS from each cell, mark visited in place with #, recurse the 4 neighbours, restore on the way out', and add the first-letter / frequency pruning.
hints: Validate the letter match at the TOP of the recursion: if this cell is out of bounds or doesn't equal word[k], return false immediately. That single guard prunes most branches.
Before recursing into neighbours, overwrite the current cell with a sentinel like '#' so the same path can't step on it again; put the original letter back after the recursion (backtrack).
Short-circuit: return true as soon as any of the 4 neighbour calls succeeds. Only start a DFS from cells equal to word[0]; optionally search for the rarer end of the word first.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each of m·n cells can launch a DFS; each DFS branches into at most 3 new directions (one neighbour is where we came from) for L levels, giving O(m·n·4^L) worst case. Space is just the recursion stack of depth ≤ L — the in-place '#' marking means no extra visited matrix, so O(L).
approaches.explanation:
Run a DFS from every cell, indexing into `word` by depth `k`. At the top of each call: if out of bounds or `board[r][c] != word[k]`, return false. If `k` has reached `word.length()`, we've matched every letter — return true. Otherwise **choose** the cell (overwrite it with `'#'`), **explore** the 4 neighbours with `k + 1`, then **un-choose** (restore the original letter), returning true if any neighbour succeeded.

**Why mark the cell — and why restore it.** The rule 'no cell reused in a path' means while we're standing on a cell, the rest of this path must treat it as off-limits. Overwriting it with `'#'` (which never equals any real letter) makes the top-of-function letter check reject it automatically — no separate visited matrix needed. But the cell is only off-limits *for the current path*: a different path should be free to use it. So the moment the recursion returns, we **restore** the original letter. That restore IS the backtracking discipline — skip it and a cell consumed on one dead-end branch stays permanently blocked, producing false negatives.

**Why check the match at the top, not before recursing.** Guarding inside the function (bounds + letter) makes the recursion self-validating: the caller can fire all four neighbour calls blindly and let each one reject itself. That keeps the code symmetric and bug-free versus pre-checking each neighbour at the call site.

**Why short-circuit and where to prune.** As soon as one neighbour returns true, the word exists — stop. We only launch a DFS where `board[r][c] == word[0]`, skipping doomed starts. A strong extra: count letter frequencies in the board versus the word and bail early if the board lacks enough of some letter; and if `word[0]` is more common than `word[-1]`, reverse `word` so the search tree branches less at the root. These don't change the big-O but slash real runtimes.
approaches.insight: The in-place '#' marker turns the board itself into the visited set, so backtracking is just 'save letter → recurse → write letter back'. The save/restore pair is the universal grid-backtracking move; once you trust it, every maze/island/word-path problem is the same skeleton with a different success test.

java.explanation: Only launch a DFS from cells matching word[0] — a cheap prune that skips most starts.

java.line: if (k == word.length()) return true;                 // matched every letter
java.explanation: Base case: depth k reached the word's length, so every letter matched along the path.
Letter check at the TOP — a '#' (visited) cell or a mismatch fails here, making the recursion self-guarding.
CHOOSE: overwrite with a sentinel so this path can't step on the cell again — no separate visited matrix.

java.line: || dfs(board, word, r, c - 1, k + 1);   // explore 4 neighbours
java.explanation: EXPLORE: short-circuits true on the first neighbour that completes the word.
UN-CHOOSE: restore the original letter so OTHER paths may reuse this cell — the key backtracking step.

Base case: we've consumed the whole word, so a full matching path exists.

python.explanation: Top-of-function guard handles bounds, the '#' visited marker, and letter mismatch in one check.

python.explanation: EXPLORE: `or` short-circuits, so we stop the moment one direction succeeds.
UN-CHOOSE: write the letter back so sibling paths can legally use this cell again.

diagrams.caption: Cells flip to '#' as the path enters them (highlighted) and would flip back on backtrack. Row shown flattened for the ABCCED prefix along the top row.

edgeCases.behavior: Start matches word[0]; DFS marks '#', then k+1 == len(word) on the next call → returns true. Single-cell word handled by the base case.
A→B→C reaches the second 'B' but the only 'B' cell is already '#', so the letter check fails, the branch unwinds restoring cells, and all starts fail → false.

pitfalls: Forgetting to restore the cell after recursion — a consumed letter stays blocked and causes false negatives.
Putting the bounds/match check at the call site instead of the top of the DFS — leads to asymmetric, buggy guards.
Not short-circuiting on the first successful neighbour — wastes work after the answer is already known.

commonMistakes: Not restoring the cell after the recursive call, so a letter used on one branch stays permanently blocked.
Omitting visited-marking entirely, allowing a path to reuse the same cell (e.g. matching 'ABCB' through one 'B').
Starting the DFS from every cell without pruning on word[0], or checking bounds at the call site instead of the top of the recursion.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Forgetting to restore the cell (no backtrack)
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If you mark a cell '#' but never write the letter back, the cell stays blocked for every other path. A valid word that needs that cell on a different route is reported missing.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
board[r][c] = '#'
found = (dfs(r+1, c, k+1) or dfs(r-1, c, k+1)
         or dfs(r, c+1, k+1) or dfs(r, c-1, k+1))
return found            # cell never restored!
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
tmp = board[r][c]
board[r][c] = '#'
found = (dfs(r+1, c, k+1) or dfs(r-1, c, k+1)
         or dfs(r, c+1, k+1) or dfs(r, c-1, k+1))
board[r][c] = tmp       # restore — the backtracking step
return found

commonMistakesDetailed.title: No visited-marking at all
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Without marking the current cell, the recursion can step back onto it, reusing one cell to satisfy two letters — wrongly matching words like 'ABCB' through a single 'B'.
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
if board[r][c] != word[k]:
    return False
tmp, board[r][c] = board[r][c], '#'            # block reuse this path
ok = (dfs(r+1, c, k+1) or dfs(r-1, c, k+1)
      or dfs(r, c+1, k+1) or dfs(r, c-1, k+1))
board[r][c] = tmp
return ok

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Checking bounds at the call site
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Pre-validating each neighbour before recursing duplicates logic four times and is error-prone. Guard once at the top of the DFS so the recursion is self-validating.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
if (r + 1 < m && board[r+1][c] == word.charAt(k+1)) dfs(board, word, r+1, c, k+1);
if (c + 1 < n && board[r][c+1] == word.charAt(k+1)) dfs(board, word, r, c+1, k+1);
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
if (r < 0 || c < 0 || r >= m || c >= n || board[r][c] != word.charAt(k)) return false;
// ...then recurse into all 4 neighbours unconditionally

followupVariations.title: Word Search II
followupVariations.hint: Many words at once → build a Trie of the word list and DFS the grid once, pruning by Trie nodes instead of restarting per word.

followupVariations.title: Number of Islands
followupVariations.hint: Same 4-directional grid DFS, but flood-fill connected land — no backtracking restore since cells stay consumed.

followupVariations.title: Surrounded Regions
followupVariations.hint: DFS from the borders marking reachable cells, then flip the rest — grid traversal with sentinel marking, like the '#' trick.

followupVariations.title: Longest Increasing Path in a Matrix
followupVariations.hint: Grid DFS again, but add memoization since paths can be revisited freely (no no-reuse constraint) — DFS + cache, not backtracking.

patternNote: Canonical Grid DFS + Backtracking (choose → explore → un-choose) with in-place visited-marking. Recognise it whenever you trace a path through a matrix under adjacency and no-reuse rules. The mark-on-enter / restore-on-exit skeleton also drives Word Search II (add a Trie), rat-in-a-maze, and unique-path enumeration problems.
